blocks.h: Why do consecutive codes differ by one bit?
p: Going from i to i+1 turns `t` trailing 1s of i into 0s and flips the 0 above them to 1, so `i ^ (i+1)` is `2^(t+1) - 1`. XORing that value with its own right shift leaves exactly one set bit, `2^t`. So the Gray codes of i and i+1 differ in a single bit. For n = 3 the sequence is `000`, `001`, `011`, `010`, `110`, `111`, `101`, `100`; each neighbour differs in one bit, and the last differs from the first in one bit too (cyclic).

89.takeaway: Gray code has a closed form: `i ^ (i >> 1)`; the sequence reflects and flips one bit at a time.

Meaning

p: `prices = [7,1,5,3,6,4]`: positive steps are 1→5 (+4) and 3→6 (+3).

blocks.h: Why is adding every positive step optimal?
p: Any profit from buying on day a and selling on day b equals the sum of the daily deltas between a and b. Taking only the positive deltas drops every negative one, which is the most any set of non-overlapping trades could keep. And since we can sell and re-buy on the same day, there is no cost to splitting a rising run into one-day trades: 1→3→6 gives the same as buying at 1 and selling at 6.
Problem 121 allows a single trade, so you must track the minimum price so far; here the number of trades is unlimited, so local gains add up.

bullets: Time: O(n).
Space: O(1).

122.takeaway: With unlimited transactions, profit is the sum of all positive day-to-day price differences: a greedy one-pass solution.
